title: Reducing Cognitive Load by Mixing Auditory and Visual Presentation Modes https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1995-38914-001
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page covers Mousavi, Low, and Sweller's foundational 1995 study on split-attention and modality effects, one of the empirical pillars of cognitive load theory. Across six experiments using geometry problems, the authors show that presenting related information in a mixed auditory-visual mode (e.g. a diagram shown visually with an accompanying spoken explanation) produces significantly better learning than presenting all of it visually (e.g. a diagram plus written text). The hypothesised mechanism is that using both auditory and visual working memory effectively expands total working memory capacity, easing the burden of split attention -- the difficulty of mentally integrating separated sources of related information. Notably, the advantage held even in conditions where the auditory and visual material could not be processed simultaneously, suggesting the benefit comes from increased capacity under dual-mode presentation rather than simultaneity itself. Barton highlights the authors' broader argument: instructional design that ignores cognitive load factors like this is likely to be deficient, a claim that helped establish cognitive load theory as central to instructional design research.
points: Presenting related information through both auditory and visual channels (e.g. diagram plus spoken explanation) improves learning compared to an all-visual presentation.
The benefit is explained by expanded effective working memory capacity when both auditory and visual channels are used, easing the split-attention problem.

Teachers can increase students' working memory capacity by presenting information using a mixed auditory and visual mode. This approach is particularly useful when students have to split their attention between multiple sources of information that need to be mentally integrated

The studies presented in the source demonstrate the benefits of a mixed auditory and visual presentation mode over a single (visual) mode. The results hold even when the auditory and visual material cannot be processed simultaneously

Six experiments using geometry problems demonstrate that a mixed auditory-visual presentation significantly improves learning outcomes compared to a purely visual approach, even when simultaneous processing is not possible
This 1995 Journal of Educational Psychology article explores how presenting information using mixed auditory and visual modes reduces cognitive load in learning

The authors hypothesize that using multiple sensory channels expands effective working memory capacity, thus mitigating the negative effects of split attention -- the difficulty of integrating information from separate sources
